name: Grindcore
about: Grindcore was invented in the English Midlands in the mid-1980s, when Napalm Death fused the speed of hardcore punk and the crust of Discharge with the blast beat and the guttural vocals of early death metal. Scum (1987) set the terms: songs of a few seconds, political rage, a wall of distortion and drums faster than seemed possible. Repulsion and Terrorizer in the United States and Carcass in Liverpool pushed it toward death metal and gore, and Brutal Truth, Assück and Nasum carried it through the 1990s. Discordance Axis and Pig Destroyer around 2000 made it strange and literary, Agoraphobic Nosebleed made it a drum-machine joke, and in the 2010s Full of Hell and Cloud Rat mixed it with noise and sludge. It remains the fastest music on earth.

artists.name: Nasum
artists.why: Swedish grind at its most polished

artists.name: Discordance Axis
artists.why: cerebral, science-fiction grind from New Jersey

albums.title: Scum
albums.why: Two different lineups, twenty-eight songs including the one-second You Suffer, and the birth of a genre on an Earache debut nothing has surpassed for sheer novelty.

albums.title: From Enslavement to Obliteration
albums.why: Lee Dorrian's bellow, Bill Steer's riffs and Mick Harris's blast beats on the follow-up that made Scum's accident a method.

albums.title: Horrified
albums.why: Recorded in 1986 and released three years later, the Michigan band's only album is the blast-beat death-grind blueprint that Napalm Death themselves acknowledged.

albums.title: World Downfall
albums.why: Pete Sandoval, Oscar Garcia and Jesse Pintado made one album before Morbid Angel claimed half the band, and it is grindcore's most perfectly produced record.

albums.title: Reek of Putrefaction
albums.why: Medical-dictionary lyrics, pitch-shifted vocals and a mix so murky it was almost formless; John Peel loved it and goregrind was born.

albums.title: A Holocaust in Your Head
albums.why: Dean Jones and Phil Vane's dual vocals over crust-punk grind, the Ipswich band's debut is the anarcho-punk wing of the style at its peak.

albums.title: Face Up to It!
albums.why: Nottingham's Heresy played hardcore at grind velocity with straight-edge politics, a key link between British thrash punk and Napalm Death.

albums.title: Anticapital
albums.why: Fourteen songs in fourteen minutes of precise, death-metal-tinged grind with Marxist lyrics, from a Florida band that rarely wasted a note.

albums.title: Extreme Conditions Demand Extreme Responses
albums.why: Former Nuclear Assault bassist Dan Lilker's band brought death-metal weight and noise experiments to grind on a landmark Earache debut.

albums.title: Need to Control
albums.why: Sludge, drone and a Germs cover stretched grindcore's boundaries on the band's second album, with a video that entered the Guinness book.

albums.title: Inhale/Exhale
albums.why: Thirty-eight songs of tight, hook-laden Swedish grind, the debut that made Nasum the standard for production and precision in the style.

albums.title: Means of Existence
albums.why: Orange County's Phobia kept the crust-punk, anti-authority spirit of grind alive on a raw and relentless record.

albums.title: The Inalienable Dreamless
albums.why: Jon Chang's shriek, Rob Marton's dissonant riffs and anime-haunted lyrics on a twenty-three-minute record that is grindcore's most singular artistic statement.

albums.title: Human 2.0
albums.why: Mieszko Talarczyk's production and sharper songwriting made the Swedes' second album their most quoted, with twenty-five songs under forty minutes.

albums.title: Prowler in the Yard
albums.why: J.R. Hayes's stalker-narrative lyrics and Scott Hull's guitars, with no bassist, on the album that made grindcore disturbing rather than merely fast.

albums.title: Murderworks
albums.why: The Finnish band's third album is HM-2 buzzsaw death-grind at its most efficient, a blueprint for the Scandinavian school of the 2000s.

albums.title: Lucid Interval
albums.why: Denver's self-described hydro-grind quintet mixed technical death metal, jazz and stoner interludes on their most inventive album.

albums.title: Altered States of America
albums.why: One hundred songs in twenty minutes from Scott Hull's drum-machine project, a conceptual joke that works as a genuine assault.

albums.title: Phantom Limb
albums.why: Longer songs, thrash and sludge riffs and Hayes's bleakest writing on the trio's most accessible and most widely praised album.

albums.title: World Extermination
albums.why: Houston's Insect Warfare made one album of pure, no-frills grind before splitting, and it became an instant underground classic.

albums.title: Abuse
albums.why: Earache signed the Singapore trio on the strength of this debut, a bass-less twenty-two-minute burst that revived old-school grind's energy.

albums.title: Longhena
albums.why: Jon Chang's post-Discordance Axis band ended with a melodic, Takafumi Matsubara-driven record that reads as a grindcore swan song.

albums.title: Trumpeting Ecstasy
albums.why: Kurt Ballou's production and Nicole Dollanganger's guest vocal on the Maryland band's breakthrough, grind fused with power electronics and death metal.

albums.title: Pollinator
albums.why: Madison Marshall's screamed, personal lyrics and a melodic, almost emo undertow on the Michigan band's most complete album.
